correctness.rationale: The ratio of successive (n+1)^s a_n is 1+O((n+1)^(-2)); summing its logs, including the tail estimate, gives a_n=c(n+1)^(-s)(1+O(1/n)), c>0. The squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm is the convergent sum of (n+1)a_n^2; both commutator products are trace class with equal trace. Direct row and column multiplication gives (1). Tail summation gives K_jj asymptotic to -2(s-1)c^2(j+1)^(1-2s)/(2s-1); for fixed sufficiently large i, K_ij is O_i((j+1)^(-s)), so the normalized entries tend to zero as O_i((j+1)^(-1/2)). For v_j=e_j-2e_(j+1)+e_(j+2), Rv_j has only two coordinates and R*v_j has its first j+1 coordinates equal to the second weight difference δ_j. The given ratio gives δ_j=O(a_j/(j+1)^2), and subtracting the exact squared norms leaves 2s a_j^2/(j+1)+O(a_j^2/(j+1)^2). The remote cross-term is minus δ_j times the coordinate sum of R*v_i, and normalizes to O_i((j+1)^(-3/2)). In each sign one can choose arbitrarily many indices successively so that every normalized absolute row sum off the diagonal is less than 1, proving definite subspaces of arbitrarily large dimension and hence infinite inertia by compact self-adjoint spectral theory. Finite prefix changes cause no issue, and (n+β)^(-s) has the required ratio. The supplied checker.py and its recorded 182 diagnostics were inspected, not executed; the all-dimensions claim is proved analytically, not by those checks. Reference 3 has a non-substantive bibliographic error: Rhaly's Terraced matrices is Bull. London Math. Soc. 21 (1989), 399–406; Houston J. Math. 15 (1989), 137–146 is p-Cesàro matrices.

value.rationale: A qualitative failure of hyponormality leaves open how many directions have each sign, even for a compact trace-zero commutator. The two infinite indices give a structural answer across the natural power-decay regime beyond the ordinary Cesàro exponent and tolerate second-order ratio perturbations. No claim is made about eigenvalue asymptotics or the endpoint s=1.
